analysis.one_liner: Bars the EPA from issuing pollution rules unless all underlying science is posted online for independent replication.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 237-190 on November 19, 2014, almost entirely along party lines, and it died in the Senate committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would forbid the EPA from proposing, finalizing, or even publishing any risk assessment, standard, or regulation unless every piece of scientific and technical information behind it — including raw data, computer code, and models — is identified and posted online in a way that allows full independent reproduction of the research [S2] [S4] [S5]. On its face this is a transparency rule. Its practical effect is that EPA could no longer rely on major public-health studies whose underlying data is confidential, such as long-running studies of air pollution built on private patient health records, so rules protecting people from pollution would be much harder or impossible to finalize. The House passed it on November 19, 2014, 237-190, with 229 of 233 Republicans in favor and 189 of 201 Democrats opposed [S8] [S9]. The Senate received it the next day and referred it to its environment committee, which never acted before the Congress ended [S7].
analysis.who_benefits: Industries facing costly EPA limits on air and water pollution — chemicals, manufacturing, power generation — gain because a rule the agency cannot fully document online cannot be finalized, and even finalized rules become vulnerable to legal challenge. The bill was backed by 53 House Republicans and no Democrats [S6] [S8].

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires that all scientific and technical information relied on for any EPA risk assessment, standard, limitation, regulation, or guidance be specifically identified and publicly available online, sufficient for independent analysis and substantial reproduction of research results [S2] [S4] [S5].

For a regulated industry, that means a costly new pollution limit can be attacked on process grounds: if any underlying dataset, code, or model is not posted — for example, health-study data that is confidential by law — the rule's legal footing is undermined [S2] [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who live near pollution sources. If the EPA cannot use landmark long-term health studies built on confidential patient records, the agency loses the scientific basis for limits on air toxics, particulate pollution, and similar hazards, and people bear the resulting exposure. Publicly funded researchers whose data includes private medical information would also lose the ability to inform regulation.
analysis.who_pays_short: People exposed to air and water pollution

drawbacks.text: The bill's central mechanism would disqualify much of the epidemiological science behind existing pollution rules, because the key studies rely on confidential patient health data that cannot legally be posted online; the text exempts only information whose disclosure is prohibited by law, which does not solve the problem that the EPA could no longer treat that data as sufficient support for a rule [S2] [S5].

Even the bill's stated goal — that publicly funded science behind regulation should be open to scrutiny — is a fair one, and an honest supporter would acknowledge the bill went further than transparency, effectively requiring the government to discard private health records it is forbidden to publish.

The bill covered every 'covered action' — risk and hazard assessments, criteria documents, standards, limitations, guidance — not just major rules, so it could freeze routine scientific work as well as regulations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency principle sounds reasonable, but the bill's design defeats its own stated purpose: the largest body of evidence on air pollution's health effects is confidential patient data that no online posting can ever satisfy. The likely result is fewer and weaker pollution protections, with the costs borne by people breathing the air, not by the industries whose compliance costs would fall. The Senate never took it up, so those costs never materialized in this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a near party-line vote of 237-190, but the Senate's environment committee never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. David Schweikert (R-AZ) on February 6, 2014, with 53 cosponsors, all Republicans [S1] [S6] [S7].
The House Science, Space, and Technology Committee ordered it reported by voice vote on June 24, 2014, and formally reported it on November 12 [S7].

Before final passage, the House rejected a Democratic motion to recommit that would have exempted EPA regulations protecting communities in emergencies — pandemics, toxic chemical releases, or attacks — by a vote of 196-230, with every Democrat voting yes and every Republican voting no [S7] [S8].
Final passage came on November 19, 2014, 237-190: 229 of 233 Republicans voted yes, 8 of 201 Democrats voted yes [S9].

The Senate received the bill on November 20, 2014, and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which took no further action before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA's existing pollution rules stayed on a normal footing, so the public kept protections the bill would have jeopardized; the industries that would have gained a tool to challenge those rules did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities relying on EPA pollution protections

sides.party_line_note: The fight split almost perfectly by party: on final passage, 229 of 233 Republicans voted yes and 8 of 201 Democrats did; on the Democratic motion to recommit, all 196 yes votes were Democrats and all 230 no votes were Republicans [S8] [S9].

industries.note: These industries face the costliest EPA limits. By requiring every data point, code, and model behind a rule to be posted online, the bill gives them a way to tie up or defeat rules on process grounds, at the public's expense in pollution exposure.

Epidemiologists whose studies rely on confidential patient records — the foundation of modern air-pollution science — could no longer support EPA regulation, devaluing decades of publicly funded health research.
The agency could not propose, finalize, or even publish a covered assessment or guidance without fully posted data and code, freezing both major rules and routine scientific documents.

industries.industry: Law firms and compliance consultancies serving regulated industries
industries.note: New data-posting requirements and litigation over whether each rule meets them would generate years of challenge work billed to regulated clients and, ultimately, to the public.
